title: Calorimetry
subtitle: Track heat through a temperature change
review: Calorimetry uses a measured temperature change to track heat transfer. A sample that warms absorbs heat; a sample that cools releases heat. Specific heat tells you how much energy is needed to warm one gram of a substance by one degree Celsius.
recap: From earlier work: identify the sample, keep mass units consistent, and subtract in the order final minus initial. A temperature change of 1 °C has the same size as a change of 1 K.
directions: Answer on this sheet. Use a calculator. Show the equation, substitution with units, and final answer in each work box. Report calculated answers to three significant figures. Brackets give numeric self-checks only.
rubric: 5-point practice rubric: complete attempt 2 • visible work and units 2 • reasoning 1
equation_note: q = heat (J) • m = mass (g) • c = specific heat [J/(g·°C)] • ΔT = temperature change (°C). Water: c = 4.18 J/(g·°C). No phase changes in these calculations.

questions.prompt: Two water samples rise by the same temperature. One has twice the mass of the other. Which absorbs more heat? Explain without calculating.
questions.answer: The sample with twice the mass absorbs twice as much heat. For the same substance and temperature change, q is proportional to m.

questions.prompt: A hot metal sample cools in water. For the METAL, is ΔT positive or negative? Is q positive or negative? Explain what the sign means.
questions.answer: Both ΔT and q are negative for the metal: its final temperature is lower and heat leaves the metal.

questions.prompt: Label A–C using thermometer, insulated cup, and water. Then state why insulation matters when measuring heat transfer.
questions.answer: A thermometer; B water; C insulated cup. Insulation reduces heat transfer with the surroundings, so the measured change better represents the exchange being studied.

questions.prompt: A 50.0 g water sample warms from 20.0 °C to 30.0 °C. Find ΔT and q for the water.
Each 10.0 g sample receives the same heat. Complete the last column with greatest, middle, or smallest temperature rise. Explain one choice.
questions.answer: Aluminum: middle; copper: greatest; water: smallest. With equal q and m, a smaller c produces a larger ΔT.

questions.prompt: A 50.0 g sample absorbs 450. J and warms from 20.0 °C to 30.0 °C. Calculate its specific heat. Which material in question 5 is the best match?
questions.answer: ΔT = 10.0 °C. c = q/(mΔT) = 450. J / [(50.0 g)(10.0 °C)] = 0.900 J/(g·°C), matching aluminum in the supplied table.

questions.prompt: A student says, “The water warmed up, so the metal must have gained heat too.” Correct the claim. Assume the metal and water exchange heat only with each other.
questions.answer: The metal loses heat while the water gains heat. Under the stated assumption, their heat transfers have equal magnitude and opposite signs. A warmer final water sample does not mean both substances gained heat.

questions.prompt: A 0.100 kg water sample warms from 20.0 °C to 35.0 °C. Convert the mass to grams, calculate q in joules, and convert q to kilojoules. Describe the transfer as endothermic or exothermic for the WATER. Connect to unit conversions and heat-transfer signs.
questions.answer: 0.100 kg × 1000 g/kg = 100. g. ΔT = 15.0 °C. q = (100. g)(4.18 J/(g·°C))(15.0 °C) = +6270 J = +6.27 kJ. Endothermic for the water because it absorbs heat. Unit conversion connects to earlier mathematical tools; heat signs connect to earlier thermochemistry.

Specific heats are supplied values, not an identification database. Students may use numeric checks to troubleshoot; explanations still need their own reasoning.
